dataset_family: Single-centre Italian navigated TMS-EEG cohort (Ferreri/Rossini group; ethics approval Campus Bio-Medico University of Rome), 17 aMCI + 15 age/gender-matched controls, 13 aMCI followed 6 years (7 converters, 6 stable)
method_family: Navigated single-pulse TMS over left M1 with 32-channel EEG: TMS-evoked potentials/GMFP, event-related spectral perturbation (ERSP) and single-channel intertrial phase coherence (ITC) compared by rm-ANOVA (group tests only for aMCI vs controls); GMFP waveform metrics (peaks, aDA, sDA) and beta/gamma ITC in a LOOCV linear SVM for converters vs non-converters only
what_it_shows: Within one small TMS-EEG sample (17 aMCI vs 15 controls), TMS-evoked spectral power change (ERSP) did not differ between groups in alpha, beta or gamma, while single-channel stimulus-locked phase consistency (ITC) was lower in aMCI at a few left fronto-central channels (alpha 6 channels p=0.03-0.04, beta 3 channels p=0.048, gamma 1 channel p=0.003; group tests only). There is no aMCI-vs-control classifier. The only classifier (converters vs non-converters, n=13) used GMFP metrics and beta/gamma ITC and never entered ERSP, so no head-to-head there. No resting-state band power, no inter-channel connectivity, no graph measure and no complexity measure is computed anywhere in the paper.
why: Identity: the PDF is Ferreri F, Guerra A, Vollero L, ... Corbetta M, Rossini PM (2021), Front Aging Neurosci 13:737281, doi 10.3389/fnagi.2021.737281. Title and authors match the P-522 block. I read the whole extract up to the References (pp.1-11, including the Supplementary Figure 1 legend). The statement needs network, connectivity or complexity measures shown to outperform conventional spectral band power for MCI discrimination. P-522 contains no measure from either class, for four reasons. (1) The power measure is TMS-evoked ERSP: a baseline-normalised, event-related change in spectral power in a +/-1 s window around each TMS pulse (p.3). It is not conventional (resting) band power, and no resting EEG was recorded. Baseline normalisation removes the tonic power level (for example slowing) that conventional band power measures, so a null ERSP does not show that conventional band power would fail in this sample. (2) The measure that succeeds is ITC, phase consistency across trials at single channels. The authors define it as 'an event-phase indicator function strictly related to the concept of signal synchronization' (p.9). It quantifies no relation between channels or regions, so it is not a connectivity, network/graph or complexity measure. Their account of cortico-basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical loop synchronization is interpretation, not a measured quantity. The intro's phrase 'effective connectivity of the somatosensory network' (p.2) names no connectivity metric; the measures actually computed are TEP/GMFP, ERSP and ITC, and sLORETA was 'for the illustrative purposes' (p.4). (3) The aMCI-vs-control comparison uses group rm-ANOVAs only: no classifier, AUC or accuracy. The ITC differences are topographically sparse (FDR-adjusted post hoc per methods p.4) in 32 people, and the authors call the results preliminary (p.10). (4) The only discrimination analysis is converters vs non-converters (7 vs 6, LOOCV linear SVM). Its features were GMFP peaks, aDA, sDA and beta/gamma ITC. ERSP was never entered, because the converter analysis was restricted to measures and channels that differed between aMCI and controls (p.4), so that analysis has no power comparator either. Its best feature, sDA, is a GMFP waveform-stability (amplitude-variability) measure, not connectivity. The study therefore shows a pattern of evoked amplitude null / evoked phase-locking significant. That is an analogy to the statement, not an instance of it. I rate it 'no' rather than 'partly' because the partly rule covers a different comparator OR a different population, whereas here both compared measure classes and the missing discrimination outcome are all outside the statement. If the operator chose to treat stimulus-locked phase synchrony as a connectivity-type measure, the most it could earn is 'partly' (group differences only, against evoked rather than conventional power). It is never full support, and the finder agreed it must not be counted as full support. Narrowed: the packet has no round-20 narrowed wording (verdict 'fails'), so n/a. The descriptive restatement floated in the round-20 reasoning (connectivity, network or microstate measures that separate MCI) would not fit either, because ITC is none of those. Independence: this is a single-centre Italian TMS-EEG cohort, with authors from Padua, Rome and Kuopio. It shares no authors, site or sample with P-553 (Seoul/Guri, Korea; Kim, Min, Park), P-501 (Detroit/Michigan; Deng, Kavcic, Giordani, Li), P-463 (Hokuto/Kumagaya, Japan; Valladolid group) or P-480 (Florence PREVIEW; Lassi, Mazzoni, Sorbi, Grippo, Bessi). I checked page 1 of each supporter's PDF. It is not a preprint: it is a peer-reviewed Frontiers original research article, published 22 Nov 2021. Extraction note: the extract fuses F-statistic degrees of freedom ('F130' = F(1,30); 'F621,860' = F(62,1860); 'F31,930' = F(31,930)). The verdict does not depend on this decoding. The quotes below normalise ligatures, typographic quotes and multiplication signs to ASCII and otherwise follow the extract.

quotes.quote: A total of 17 patients with MCI were recruited based on the diagnostic criteria for aMCI (Albert et al., 2011). The control group (CO) consisted of 15 age- and gender-matched healthy subjects.

Electroencephalography signals were segmented in the time windows of +/-1 s around the stimulus and preprocessed according to the previous studies ... To evaluate the event-related changes in the frequency domain, the event-related spectral perturbation (ERSP) and intertrial coherence (ITC) were calculated (Delorme and Makeig, 2004). We extracted the average ERSP and ITC for alpha (8-13 Hz), beta (13.5-30 Hz), and gamma (30.5-80 Hz, excluding 45-55 Hz band due to notch filtering application) frequency bands.

The frequency analysis showed comparable ERSP values between the aMCI and controls in all the frequency bands, as demonstrated by the non-significant factor "group" (F130 = 0.08, p = 0.78) and the lack of "group"x"frequency"x"channel" (F621,860 = 0.849, p = 0.79), "group"x"frequency" (F260 = 1.757, p = 0.18), and "group"x"channel" (F31,930 = 0.707, p = 0.88) interactions.

Conversely, ITC differed between the groups, as the significant "group"x"frequency"x"channel" interaction (F621,860 = 1.656, p < 0.001). The rm ANOVAs conducted for each frequency band revealed topographically specific differences in ITC in the alpha ("group"x"channel" interaction: F31,930 = 1.809, p = 0.005), beta (F31,930 = 1.616, p = 0.02) and gamma (F31,930 = 1.742, p < 0.01) bands. Post hoc analyses indicated lower alpha ITC in the aMCI than controls in C3, FC5, F7, T7, P7 (p = 0.03), and FC1 (p = 0.04); lower beta ITC in C3, FC1, and FC5 (p = 0.048); and lower gamma ITC in FC1 (p = 0.003) (Figure 2B).

Due to the small size of pAD-MCI and npAD-MCI subsamples, we did not look for any possible difference between them and instead we focused on the channels in which there was a significant [false discovery rate (FDR), adjusted] post hoc difference between the aMCI and controls.

To evaluate the GMFP features (# of peaks, aDA, and sDA) and beta and gamma ITC as the predictors of conversion to AD, we trained a binary, linear classification model by using support vector machines, dual stochastic gradient descent, and ridge regularization.

our analyses in the frequency domain showed a selective ITC disruption and a clear ERSP preservation in the stimulated cortex of the whole aMCI group. This result is particularly intriguing: indeed, ERSP measures the modulation of amplitude induced by a specific event, whereas ITC is an event-phase indicator function strictly related to the concept of signal synchronization in the brain (Delorme and Makeig, 2004).

The parameters showing the highest sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy were sDA and gamma ITC. In particular, sDA (cutoff = 0.86) demonstrated a sensitivity of 100% (95% CI: 72-100%), specificity of 100% (95% CI: 69-100%), and accuracy of 100% (95% CI: 77-100%), while gamma ITC (cutoff = 0.20) showed a sensitivity of 86% (95% CI: 49-97%), specificity of 83% (95% CI: 44-97%), and accuracy of 85% (95% CI: 58-96%).
This study has some limitations. First, since the number of participants was low, the results should be considered as preliminary.
